newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: ANZ SAYS COMPETITION, NOT COLLUSION, RESPONSIBLE FOR CUT
The ANZ Bank says its cut in home loan interest rates on Friday didn't go any further because it took into account an earlier cut.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission is investigating the decision by the four major banks to reduce their home loan rates by the same amount -- point-three-five of one per cent -- after the Reserve Bank cut offical rates by a half-a-per cent.
But the ANZ Bank says competition, not collusion, forced it to match the rates offered by the other three major banks.
ANZ spokesman, Rob Gerrand, says the ANZ didn't go further because of an earlier cut in February of point-seven of one per cent.
PM MUST SHOW HE HAS A GOOD HEART, AND APOLOGISE
The Vice-President of the South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission says John Howard will be diminished as a person if he fails to apologise to Aboriginal people today.
The Prime Minister is under pressure to open the Australian Reconciliation Convention with an apology for policies which led to the forcible removal of indigenous children from their families.
Dr Alex Boraine says Mr Howard should express, on behalf of the Federal Government, his sorrow for the hurt the policies caused.
Dr Boraine says he's sure Mr Howard has a good heart, but says the Prime Minister needs to show that.
The Federal Opposition also has urged the Prime Minister to show some generosity of spirit, and apologise to Aborigines forcibly removed from their families.
TARIFF REPORT "SHOULD BE RELEASED ASAP"
Unions claim the final report of the Productivity Commission on car tariffs will be delayed for several weeks.
The Commission's draft recommendation that tariffs be cut to five-per cent by 2004 have been strongly opposed by car makers, industry unions and the South Australian and Victorian Governments.
Paul Noack, of the Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union, says the report should be publicly released to allow debate.
He claims only the South Australian and Victorian Premiers will be given confidential copies, while unions and other political parties will miss out.
HERRON: CASH UNLIKELY FOR STOLEN GENERATION
Indigenous Australians affected by a policy which saw indigenous children forcibly taken from their families will find out on Wednesday what the Federal Government will do for them.
Cabinet is considering its response to the Human Rights Commission's stolen children inquiry, and will formally respond on Wednesday.
The report has urged the Government to make a formal apology and pay compensation to those Aborigines taken from their parents between 1910 and 1970.
But Federal Aboriginal Affairs Minister, John Herron, says cash compensation is highly unlikely.
Senator Herron says while it's legitimate to ask for an apology it's not up to him to apologise.
WOOLWORTHS CHAIRMAN DIES, AGED 60
Woolworths has announced the death of its Chairman, John Illiffe.
Mr Illiffe died in a Sydney hospital on Saturday, aged 60.
He'd been in hospital for about two weeks to undergo surgery.
Mr Illiffe had been Woolworths Chairman since November 1995.
He was also chairman of GIO, and was a former President of the Sydney Organising Committee for the Olympic Games.
Woolworths' John Phillips, who's now acting Chairman, has paid tribute to Mr Illiffe, saying he made a substantial contribution to the company.
QANTAS DISPUTE BACK IN INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS COMMISSION
Qantas is back in the Industrial Relations Commission this afternoon over a dispute with its workers.
The Australian Services Union says Qantas sacked 20 workers in Brisbane and three at Coolangatta last week without fulfilling requirements of the company's Enterprise Bargaining Agreement.

The State Secretary of the Union, Janice Mayes, says Qantas breached the agreement by failing to notify the union of the sackings, not providing a reason for the job losses or negotiating with the union with a view to re-locating the workers.
The case will be heard in the Australian Industrial Relations Commission this afternoon.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
